articles.title: We Must Talk about Denuclearizing Israel
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: There is a simple action DSA can take to dramatically change the relationship between the United States and the genocidal regime in Israel. Start talking about their nukes. Openly, aggressively. Denounce Israel as a rogue nuclear state. Since Israel began developing its nuclear program in the 1950s, its nuclear capabilities have remained the subject of longstanding secrecy and diplomatic silence. The U.S. government has refused to acknowledge Israeli weapons for a variety of reasons; a big one is that a Presidential determination would trigger the stiff sanctions in Sec. 102(B) of the Arms Export Control Act. By acknowledging and denouncing Israel’s nuclear arsenal, DSA can force political recognition of these weapons and inspire action, such as imposing sanctions on Israel. Furthermore, the non-recognition of Israeli nuclear weapons creates a political asymmetry in which Iranians become the “bad” guys for wanting to deter Israeli nuclear aggression. If Iran wanted to acquire such weapons, it would not be doing so in a vacuum as though a bunch of mavericks had suddenly introduced nuclear weapons into the Middle East for the first time. Israel already possesses them and is obsessed with destroying the Iranian state. In other words, the public logic of the aggression against Iran, which was launched with the atomically thin justification of denying Iran nuclear weapons, depends upon the continued non-recognition of Israel’s own nuclear arsenal. The imperialist line is even more absurd given that at least until the February 2026 U.S. assassination of Ayatollah Khamenei, Iran had a fatwa (a religious ruling) against building such weapons. Moreover, what is known of Israel’s nuclear policy is that it is alone in the world in continuing to contemplate weapons use against its non-nuclear neighbors explicitly. Yet, this is not the half of it. Israel’s nuclear arsenal helps explain several otherwise puzzling aspects of the U.S.-Israel “special relationship.” Why does the genocidal regime in Tel Aviv exercise such extraordinary influence over U.S. policy? Why do countries around the world, despite widespread disgust at Israeli and American genocide and aggression, have been unwilling or unable to forcefully intervene? Why do the weaker nations of the world allow international law to be discarded so casually? What would be needed to stop Israel for good? The Israeli nuclear arsenal is a key under-discussed factor. The U.S. socialist movement, including our elected leaders, is not anywhere near where we need to be in terms of formal influence over public policy around these issues, yet this shouldn’t mean total silence. We have a bully pulpit from which to speak, and we must engage all levers of power to stop the genocidal Israeli grab for lebensraum. U.S. support for Israel cannot simply be explained by some timeless affinity with Jewish people, given the history of U.S. antisemitism. There are sticky factors that are tying American imperialism to this specific colonial outpost, and a big one is the bomb. Nuclear containment with flowers The American state consists of both a rational part and an ideological part. There must be something that is firmly convincing the rational actors to let the ideologues have their way. Israel is a tiny nuclear state with a huge victim complex that is highly militarily vulnerable should its subsidies be cut off. It is unique in that it is the only nuclear state that is not formally acknowledged. A formal admission by the U.S. that Israel is nuclear-armed would trigger domestic sanctions and begin major reorientations in the region. Of all the countries that have acquired nukes after the 1967 Non-Proliferation Treaty cutoff (the DPRK, India, Israel, and Pakistan), Pakistan and the DPRK are subject to sanctions. India was subject to stricter sanctions, but craftily cut a deal with the U.S. in 2008, and more of those sanctions are being removed . Israel alone has avoided sanctions entirely. Apartheid South Africa, a nuclear collaborator with Israel, also attempted this trick, but when the Afrikaner regime finally collapsed, they dismantled their small stockpile of nuclear weapons to avoid letting them fall into the hands of Black Africans. Notwithstanding the occasional slip-up, U.S. politicians do not acknowledge Israel’s nuclear status, and Israeli politicians are usually ( but not always ) oblique about it. This suppresses most official discussion of nuclear policy around Israel, though academics and journalists will sometimes speak up on the margins. Congresspeople do not discuss the issue publicly since it goes against the U.S.’s unofficial but rigid nuclear policy position of strategic ambiguity regarding Israel’s weapons program. It is a strange game where everyone knows the truth but does not speak it out loud, leaving Israel’s status suspended in the air. It is thought that Israel has boosted fission nuclear weapons and potentially untested thermonuclear and neutron bomb designs based on research data from its collaborations with France and South Africa. Modern boosted fission weapons are an order of magnitude more powerful than the two comparatively simple and morally shocking 15-20 kiloton city killers that America detonated in Japan. To give a sense of proportion, while American nuclear arsenals have had bombs up to 25 megatons in the 1960s, our modern strategy focuses on a greater number of lower-yield weapons in the hundred kiloton range. For the most part, this strategy is more efficient at destroying a given area than a larger bomb of equivalent strength (though the big ones are still useful when used with inaccurate missiles). In order for a research program to develop reliable weapon designs, it is crucial to obtain accurate explosive test data. Despite U.S. denials, it is likely that Israel collected test data in partnership with South Africa; a part of a test sequence was observed in the 1979 VELA satellite incident when a break in the cloud cover revealed a tell-tale double flash over the Southern Indian Ocean. Seymour Hersh wrote there were three tests, and the one that was caught by VELA was a low-yield nuclear artillery shell according to multiple unnamed Israeli government sources in his 1991 book “The Samson Option.” (Hersh, p. 271) Said French nuclear physicist Francis Perrin, who participated in discussions about building the reactor, “We thought the Israeli bomb was aimed at the Americans…. Not to launch it against America but to say, ‘If you don’t want to help us in a critical situation, we will require you to help us. Otherwise we will use our bombs.'” (Hersh, p. 40). There is an unfortunate realist logic to Israel’s nuclear policy. Since the country is so small, it cannot absorb a ground invasion force the way Russia, for example, has been able to historically. Therefore, since it is nuclear-armed, Israel has implied it will use its nuclear weapons in a first strike against non-nuclear states should it fear for the life of the state. A nuclear attack in the region would slaughter innocent people in the hundreds of thousands, millions, or tens of millions in a horrific manner . Additionally, Israel is located in an energy-rich region with critical shipping lanes. Such an attack would likely target economic targets like oil fields across the Middle East, obliterate them, and contaminate them with radioactive fallout. Shipping lanes would be disrupted, with ports destroyed or even tight geographic features like the Suez Canal could be damaged. Firestorms started by nuclear explosions could smoke into the stratosphere , which would linger for some time. The reduced sunlight would degrade agricultural output over a wide area (an effect termed “nuclear autumn”), creating famines that could be even more deadly than direct war damage. This is the kind of power the Tel Aviv Reich wields. It helps explain why the international community has barely lifted a finger to help the Palestinian people in the midst of a genocide where one 2025 projection estimates 680,000 Palestinians may have already perished from all causes. In addition to all the direct sticks and carrots American diplomats have undoubtedly deployed behind closed doors, they can also appeal to reason: You wouldn’t want them to go nuclear, would you? Such a situation as outlined above would be much worse for the economy than the current self-induced crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, one might think that American planners would attempt to mitigate the risk of nuclear war—and mitigate it they do. You can see this in their harsh and unrelenting treatment of Iran, where they constantly talk about preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon. While I don’t believe this is their only motivating factor, nor that their treatment is justifiable on a moral or legal basis, it is true that they routinely set back Iranian nuclear chemistry capabilities with varying degrees of effectiveness. Iran bears American aggression because they do not possess a nuclear weapon. During the Korean War, North Korea had about 20% of its population wiped out in the 1950s by American aggression and was constantly antagonized until they acquired a nuclear deterrent and now appear to be safe. By contrast, Libya surrendered its nuclear program, and its leader Gaddafi was sodomized with a bayonet after America secured the safety of a militant insurgency from the air. Three different countries contradicting American interests, three different nuclear statuses, three different outcomes. Iran has nuclear potential and is resisting; Libya surrendered and was defeated; the DPRK succeeded and is secure. That doesn’t mean acquiring a nuclear weapon is some unalloyed good. It defers one immediate state-wide risk for a potentially wide-area or world-wide one that gets bigger with each country that acquires them. Israel offers a mirror perspective to examine. They already possess nuclear weapons. If America treated Israel like we do Iran, such as by routinely assassinating their citizens and invading their airspace, Israel would probably perform a nuclear strike, so that approach is ruled out. If Iran treated Israel like America treats Iran, that too could trigger a nuclear launch. Hence, Iran is very careful about calibrating its actions and signaling its position in the escalation ladder when it does act. It’s not in America’s interest for Israel to wage nuclear war in a highly sensitive region. So how does America “contain” Israel? With flowers instead of swords, in what is frequently termed a “bear hug.” America provides a conventional security guarantee to avoid existential Israeli anxiety that stems from their extensive history of criminality and territorial vulnerability. The word “anxiety” is important because Israeli anxieties may become detached from reality, but America’s military commitment must scale with them lest they launch the nukes. After Operation Al-Aqsa Flood on October 7, 2023, the settler-colony’s paranoia has become all-consuming, attacking everyone and everything around it viciously and without conscience. The Israeli public’s blood lust gives Nazi Germany a run for its money—in 2024, 73% of the citizenry, amidst a horrific slaughter of children, thought that the job the military was doing was “about right” or “not far enough.” With Israel’s international reputation in tatters, and with Israel’s domestic politics stabilized by expansionary war, they are attempting to complete and solidify their conquests with all possible haste, hoping that all will be forgiven, or at least tolerated, in the gleaming light of victory. American military commitments have paced Israel’s expansionist aggression and genocidal revenge. In 1956, when the Dimona research facility was still in its early phases, Bertrand Goldschmidt, who was present at a meeting of the French Atomic Energy Commission, shared,: “…They [the Israeli delegation] said that when the Americans will realize we have a nuclear capacity, they will give us the guarantee of survival. All this was decided before the Suez Affair.” (p. 39) To put it crudely, Israel has America by the balls, and America is smiling. Lest you think this is an exaggeration, in the chapter “Nuclear Blackmail” of “The Samson Option,” during the 1973 Yom Kippur War Israel was losing badly, and their military was threatening to collapse for lack of supplies. Henry Kissinger was considering letting Egypt bleed Israel a bit and then have the two sides settle for peace on more balanced terms. Instead, the Israelis raised a nuclear alert and forced him into an immediate conventional arms resupply. In a second incident, during the first Gulf War, Hersh describes how in response to Iraqi truck-mounted Scud missiles that were rumored to be loaded with chemical weapons, Israel raised a nuclear alert that lasted for weeks and visibly pointed its nuclear launchers at Iraq. In response, America offered money, patriot missile batteries, and marked Scud launchers as priority targets. It turned out the Scuds were conventionally armed. (Hersh, p. 318) The attitude of John McCone, CIA Director in 1961, was reported by Walt Elder, an executive assistant to the CIA, as, “He thought an Israeli bomb would lead to escalation and then you could just cross off oil from the Middle East for years.” (Hersh, p. 106) In February 1968, just before Israel had completed its first bomb, according to Schlomo Aronson, Henry Kissinger said to a group of Israeli scholars that the United States would not “lift a finger” to help in case of a Soviet missile attack—right after Israeli intelligence learned that four Israeli cities had been added to Soviet nuclear targeting lists. (Hersh, p. 177) There is also a historical coincidence that occludes the nuclear aspect in some discussions of the America-Israeli relationship. Around the time Israel acquired its first nuclear weapons, the country also fought and won the Six-Day War. This was the moment Israel proved itself to America and the Zionist lobby started to become included in major decisions. Anti-semitism went from highly prevalent to a no-no. Due to this timing, aggressive containment of Israel’s nukes was never on the table (though there was substantial but ineffective pressure for IAEA inspections of the Negev Nuclear Research Facility). Thus, containment with flowers was born. All the incentives align—and while American planners inside think-tanks and the military may not have particularly wanted Israel to get a nuke (though they pointedly looked the other way according to Hersh), American Zionist businesspeople with close ties to the U.S. government helped finance Israel’s acquisition of nuclear technology from France. France agreed to sell Israel a nuclear reactor in exchange for help retaining French Algeria as well as due to mutual nuclear collaboration with scientists when France was building its own weapon. While sending conventional arms to Israel helps forestall imminent use, it is something of a band-aid. Israel is still a tiny state that is unable to absorb land invasions. This causes considerable existential anxiety. If Israel were territorially bigger, this anxiety would be reduced (and it would have more natural resources, making it more self-sustaining). Thus, there is at least one rational basis for at least some U.S. planners to support the “Greater Israel” project to take over the Middle East even though there is no possible legal or moral justification for this concept. Another dismal aspect to consider is that based on the disclosures by Mordecai Vanunu, Israel likely has advanced “clean” neutron weapons that have vastly reduced fallout compared to standard designs. (Hersh, p. 199-200) This has serious implications because it increases their willingness to use nuclear weapons in proximity to nearby population centers – such as Gaza. One shouldn’t assume that just because our government supports Israel and doesn’t publicly mention their nuclear capability doesn’t mean the military doesn’t make certain considerations for it. Despite my longstanding serious grievances with the U.S. military, I don’t think they would like other countries to be freelancing nuclear war. Therefore, the deployment of naval vessels and bases around Israel possibly has a dual purpose. If Israel plays along, we use those assets to protect their territory and reduce their existential dread. If they launch nuclear missiles, those assets can be used to try to shut down their remaining launch capability, and in certain lucky cases, perhaps shoot down an impulsive limited launch, particularly if there was forewarning. If that shut-down capability is used, the “special relationship” would be over, so if there are such plans, they would only be used as a last resort. Even if they are in place, I’m not confident that the realists would win the argument over the ideologues. According to Hersh, Israel has missiles, bomber aircraft, long-range nuclear artillery shells, suitcase nukes, and nuclear landmines—it is not possible to stop them if they are really determined to use their capability. containing nuclear apartheid How can the Israeli war machine and settler-colonial project be stopped? There are some unfortunate facts. The first is that no state will intervene militarily in Israel’s territory in a way that seriously scares them for fear of inciting a nuclear strike. Conventional missile attacks have a much more limited capacity to ignite that kind of fear—air power alone is generally insufficient to overthrow a government. Iran, Lebanon, and Yemen have launched missiles and rockets, but no military has dared to cross the border to assist the internal Palestinian Resistance since the first day of Operation Al-Aqsa Flood, when resistance fighters streamed out of Gaza. The focus has been instead on containing and punishing Israeli aggression in very measured ways. The safest strategy is to aid in causing the nuclear-armed apartheid state to collapse internally via economic sanctions. However, so long as nothing is done about the nukes, they can continue to get away with applying the Dahyia doctrine of total destruction wherever they attack. The unfortunate truth is that it would take decades for a tough sanctions regime to start to make a dent in their nuclear capability. One should not expect the apartheid regime to fall quietly. When the victory comes, it is plausible that, as in the South African case, the Israeli government would destroy their own nukes rather than hand them over to Palestinians as part of shared democratic governance. We can expect the revolutionaries to have to make hard and swift decisions to attempt to avoid the worst. In the United States, we will need to do our part to support the new Palestinian government. Speak the Truth about Israeli Nuclear Weapons Iran historically did not want a nuclear weapon, but given the current unprovoked assault on Iran and the reality of Israeli nuclear weapons, and with their biggest opponent, Ayatollah Khamenei, assassinated, they would be foolish not to consider acquiring a deterrent. In response to this situation of its own making, the U.S. is considering providing civil nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia , so if Iran were to acquire a deterrent, Saudi Arabia might not be too many years behind them. This is a nightmare of nuclear proliferation that could cause other countries at odds with these powers to become interested in their own capability. The risks to the region and the world would keep increasing. There could be some positives if Iran obtained nuclear capability. For example, they could extend their nuclear umbrella to Lebanon and Gaza, much as the U.S. does for NATO allies; this would do much for curbing Israeli excesses and would give the Palestinian resistance much-needed relief from the constant onslaught of the occupation forces. An Iranian deterrent would secure the safety of Iran from invasion, provide the Palestinians with a lifeline, and contain the Greater Israel project. It might even open the door to the fall of apartheid Israel. However, these positives would come at the risk of a two-sided nuclear war in the Middle East with all that entails—including the risk of entangling other nuclear powers. The root cause of this situation is Israel’s behavior, the fact of Israel’s nuclear arsenal, and the actions of the United States. This can all be avoided if Israel were to denuclearize, which will only be possible if the United States insists on it. What is our contribution? DSA can immediately help by talking about Israeli nukes officially and pointing out the difference in how Israel and Iran are treated on this issue. This will impede American aggression against Iran and give Iran a political lifeline. I suspect that some DSA congresspeople have been reluctant to speak on this issue because of the nuclear gag. For example, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has for years maintained a very controversial position of supporting defensive weapons such as interceptor missiles for the Israeli military but not offensive weapons like guns, tanks, bombs, etc. These defensive weapons, of course, allow the Israeli military to commit crimes without taking a hit back. Recently, in concert with the Israeli government signaling they’re okay with it , she has adopted the finely threaded position that defensive weapons are good, but Israel has to pay for them. It is hard to know what someone is truly thinking, but one very charitable explanation for AOC’s bizarre position is a credible fear of Israel starting a nuclear war. U.S. government officials have been reticent to talk about Israeli nukes for the entire duration of the program, even within the confines of the intelligence agencies. On March 26, 2026, Rep. Ilhan Omar was interviewed on the subject of Israeli nukes: “We’re able to talk about what kind of nukes we have. We have always been able to talk about the nukes that exist with our allies. The fact that we can’t have a discussion on Israel’s nukes, whether they have it or whether they tried to acquire it, and how much they have… it tells you that the level of fear that exists in Washington when it comes to questioning anything Israel and its army is doing.” On May 5th, she and thirty of her colleagues, led by Rep. Joaquin Castro, presented a letter to Sec. of State Marco Rubio demanding clarity on Israel’s nuclear capability in stark terms, yet still hedged their language in terms of possibilities rather than a frank acknowledgement. She came close, but Ms. Omar and her colleagues stopped short of recognizing a reality that has been evident for decades. She did not break the taboo. Nonetheless, there is momentum on this issue. Breaking the taboo will have impacts on the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It will rearrange nuclear policy in the Middle East. It will refocus attention on the real reason for the aggression against Iran: ensuring Israel retains nuclear supremacy over its neighbors. My fellow comrades in the DSA, it is important that we continue to raise the banner of Palestine every chance we get and build pressure to disarm Israel. It is clear that this is a central challenge of our time. We must be able to push boundaries. We must defend the humanity of Palestinians and support the fall of the apartheid state as quickly as possible. We must talk about denuclearizing Israel. reference Hersh, Seymour M. The Samson Option: Israel’s Nuclear Arsenal and American Foreign Policy . 1. ed., 2. print, Random House, 1991. ISBN 0-394-57006-5

articles.title: Iceland votes against joining EU
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: On August 29, a majority of Icelanders voted against resuming accession negotiations with the European Union. In a high-turnout referendum , close to 53% of the 225,031 participants rejected the proposal, while 47% supported it. Mainstream reports emphasized that the campaign against negotiations focused on issues of agriculture and fishing. At first glance, this aligned the “No” campaign with far-right talking points in the region – reflected in congratulatory notes circulated by European right-wing leaders. According to the same reports, the “Yes” campaign centered on international policy and alignment, apparently suggesting the EU as a path to provide more stability in the face of an aggressive US administration with eyes on the Arctic’s mineral reserves. Read more: Greenland on the chessboard of US imperialism Yet progressive parties and groups also voiced opposition to joining the EU, criticizing the bloc’s political and economic agenda. While some left-wing political figures, like the Left-Green Movement’s Rósa Björk Brynjólfsdóttir, announced they would support new talks – reflecting polls indicating a significant share of their voters planned to do the same – large sections of the parties’ membership did the opposite. The Left-Green Movement’s youth, for example, opposed the referendum proposal. Together with youth members from other progressive parties, the Left-Green Movement youth activists criticized the EU’s harsh economic and migration policies, as well as its failure to act against Israel’s genocide in Gaza. “There is enough information available for left-leaning people to familiarize themselves with what the EU stands for, and it should be very clear that is not what we want,” Silja Sóley Birgisdóttir from the Socialist Party of Iceland told local media . The Socialist Party provided more information on its opposition to joining the EU ahead of the referendum. “The EU is an economic bloc and a union of states fundamentally built on capitalist economic policies, a foreign policy that serves imperialism, militarism, and Zionism, the distancing of citizens from decision-making, and the weakening of independent working-class struggle,” the party wrote. “Within the EU’s legal and regulatory framework, market laws are prioritized at the expense of the public interest,” they added, expressing concern about policies related to public education, housing, and healthcare in case of EU accession. “At the same time, the EU’s legal and regulatory framework further opens the door to privatization, competition, and the outsourcing of public services.” Progressives’ concerns regarding accession to the EU were also based on other Nordic countries’ experiences, where activists and trade unionists warned of erosion of social and labor policies as a result of EU policies. “Any attempt to maintain specific standards for the environment, health, food quality, working conditions and the like is, in the EU’s view, an example of interfering with market forces,” Danish activist and politician Karen Sunds said during a discussion on this topic organized by the Socialist Party. Read more: “We cannot eat grenades once the grains no longer grow:” European peace movements organize against militarization Critics also questioned the argument that joining the EU would bring Iceland more security, emphasizing the bloc’s militarization agenda pursues very different goals from countering concrete threats from the Trump administration. Instead, this line of argument insisted that EU leaders and institutions remain mostly aligned with the US, eyeing confrontation with Russia and China. In this context, Sunds suggested , the EU’s interest in Iceland might not rest on building a more coherent regional bloc, but instead on securing energy resources located in Arctic regions. According to Sunds, traces of this interpretation can also be found in statements by EU officials. Already a year ago, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the following on the Arctic’s strategic importance during a Nordic Council meeting: “Yes, global warming brings new and dangerous risks to the Arctic. But it also brings new responsibilities, and new opportunities. Take critical raw materials. Greenland alone holds 25 of the 34 critical materials that Europe needs – a treasure locked beneath ice and rock.”

articles.title: Clashes reignite in Sweida between government forces and Druze groups
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: At least two civilians were killed, and 10 Syrian security personnel were wounded in renewed clashes between Druze armed groups and Syrian government forces in Syria’s southern governorate of Sweida. According to media reports , the conflict erupted again in Sweida on Saturday, August 29, and continued through Monday, August 31, after the Druze armed group the National Guard blocked roads, preventing students from traveling to government-controlled examination centers north of Sweida. The National Guard, which is affiliated with Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri (known for his alignment with Israel), accused the Syrian government forces of firing a number of mortar shells against civilians. The group further claimed that a child was injured as a result of the shelling. The development signals a continued challenge to Al-Sharaa’s administration to integrate all sectarian and ethnic minorities into the state, though it came one week after finalizing the integration of the Kurds. It also exposes the volatile sectarian divisions in the post-Assad era and jeopardizes nationwide sovereignty, as the possibility of Israel’s intervention under the pretext of protecting the Druze minority looms. Read more: Israel launches airstrikes on Syria as sectarian violence continues to spiral Syria’s interim government completes Kurdish civil and military integration into its institutions The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced on Thursday, August 20, the dissolution of the armed group as an independent ​military force. Abdi also affirmed at an event in Syria’s northeastern city of Qamishli that the phase of integrating Kurdish military, security, and administrative institutions into national state institutions was complete and finished. One week later, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa issued a decree , appointing Abdi as “an advisor to the Presidency of the Republic.” With the completion of the integration process, curtains fall on the Kurds’ long-held dream of autonomy . However, the renewed sectarian clashes in Sweida, alongside the latest explosions in the Syrian capital of Damascus, and recurrent Israeli assaults underscore the prevailing security challenges in Syria. articles.title: Gloria Steinem, Feminist Icon & Ms. Magazine Co-Founder, Dies at 92
articles.content: Feminist icon Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92. According to her Instagram page, she died Wednesday “at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her.” Steinem was a tireless advocate for the social, economic and political advancement of women. Steinem co-founded Ms. magazine, the first major publication to be owned, run and written by women. She also helped found the National Women’s Political Caucus with a group of women including Shirley Chisholm, Betty Friedan and Fannie Lou Hamer. Before becoming a feminist icon, she served as director of the Independent Research Service, a nonprofit educational foundation secretly funded by the CIA . In 2013, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama. She spoke with Democracy Now! at the historic Women’s March in Washington, D.C., on January 21, 2017. We play an excerpt.

articles.title: “Catastrophic Failure”: Postal Service Whistleblower Warns Mail-In Voting Rules Could Derail Election
articles.content: An anonymous federal whistleblower has warned that the Trump administration’s new system for handling mail ballots through the U.S. Postal Service is untested, fatally flawed and likely to lead to a “catastrophic failure” if it’s implemented ahead of November’s midterm elections. This follows President Trump’s executive order in March directing his administration to create federal lists of citizens and to refuse delivery of mail-in ballots to people not on those lists. The legality of Trump’s executive order is being challenged. The new hurdles raised by the executive order for mail ballots and the rushed software system built to administer them “create this potential for grave, catastrophic failure,” says David Kligerman from Whistleblower Aid, the organization representing the whistleblower.

articles.title: “Modern-Day Poll Tax”: Dem. Texas Commissioner Slams GOP Vote to Close 92 Polling Sites
articles.content: Ahead of the November midterm elections, Republican officials in the third most populous county of Texas have voted to slash the number of polling sites by nearly one-third. Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, will have just 224 polling sites for 1.3 million voters. The change was approved in a party-line vote Tuesday, with all three of the county’s Republican commissioners voting in favor and the two Democrats opposing it. Civil rights groups including the ACLU and NAACP warn the changes will disproportionately affect voters of color. “The eyes of the nation are on Tarrant County,” says Roderick Miles Jr., a Democratic Tarrant County commissioner, who calls the voting restriction a “modern-day poll tax.”

articles.title: AI Could Revolutionize Medicine, But Humans Must Be in Charge: Researcher Shreya Johri
articles.content: As part of our ongoing series on artificial intelligence, we speak with researcher Shreya Johri, who says AI has the power to revolutionize the field of medicine, particularly in diagnosing patients. Johri is a postdoctoral fellow at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and completed her Ph.D. at Harvard Medical School in 2025. She discusses ways that new technology is improving patient care, but she says AI must be treated like an additional tool and not be given control over patient care. “Doctors have to be responsible, have to take the responsibility of this, until we are more confident we have frameworks developed that can deploy these AI models in a more responsible way,” she says.

articles.title: Germany escalates tensions with Russia, continues military exports to Israel
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: German authorities have blamed Russia for a drone attack on a cargo plane at an airport in Leipzig in early August, marking a new escalation in tensions towards the Russian Federation. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s administration summoned Russian diplomats and announced new sanctions following these accusations. Russia has denied involvement and responded by summoning the German chargé d’affaires in Moscow. “It was stressed that the German Government’s decision to use this contrived pretext to close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin is viewed as yet another step towards the complete dismantling of the bilateral relationship painstakingly built by generations of Russian and German politicians and diplomats,” the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated on September 2. “It was emphasized that Berlin deliberately resorted to an outright provocation aimed at escalating Russian-German relations.” Read more: Thousands join Berlin’s Peace Days to support antimilitarism and solidarity Back in Germany, the accusations against Vladimir Putin’s administration were followed by reassurances of unwavering support to Ukrainian authorities. German claims of hybrid warfare against EU countries rippled throughout the bloc, prompting renewed concerns from progressive analysts and activists about European rearmament – especially given Germany’s prominent role in promoting it. Germany’s support for the war in Ukraine continues to be accompanied by military cooperation with Israel. In response to a parliamentary inquiry from the left party Die Linke, the government reported it had approved military exports to the occupation entity worth approximately USD 930 million in the first half of 2026. According to Anadolu Agency, German military exports to Israel were four times higher than in 2025 and included naval projects, small arms, drones, and joint projects considered strategically important for the German armed forces. Further cooperation between German industry and Israel’s arms producers is proceeding despite the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Local peace initiatives and progressive parties have emphasized that this approach exposes the contradictions of European rearmament at the expense of public services and civilian industry. Among these voices is the Osnabrück Peace Initiative, currently campaigning to prevent a Volkswagen factory in Lower Saxony from being repurposed to produce Iron Dome components in cooperation with Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. Volkswagen, affected by Germany’s industrial crisis, is looking into pivoting toward military production – an approach European officials claim will drive the region’s reindustrialization. While the plan to partner with Rafael has faced resistance from the very beginning, company management appears eager to move forward and has approached the Lower Saxony government with a partnership proposal worth hundreds of millions of euros. Read more: Germany’s ‘summer of reforms’ to accelerate militarization Local activists have decisively rejected the false binary between unemployment and military production. They insist that authorities’ plans to launch more arms factories show they have learned nothing from past wars. In Osnabrück, which hosted arms factories during World War II and suffered Allied bombardment as a result, peace groups reiterated they would continue campaigning against the plans. “When arms factories are once again established in the city some 80 years after the last war, one can only despair at the decision-makers’ disregard for history,” they told Anadolu Agency.

articles.title: Uganda Communist League members arrested after inaugural congress
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Members of the newly formed Communist League of Uganda were arrested and allegedly subjected to severe treatment by state security forces days after the organization concluded its inaugural National Congress, according to a statement issued by the League. The Communist League of Uganda said several of its members, including Vice Chairperson Habibu Twahala, Odeke Dan, and Namususwa Patricia, were arrested on August 29, 2026, while participating in a mobilization drive. The arrests came shortly after the League held its first National Congress, marking the organization’s formal effort to establish itself as a political organization representing working-class interests in Uganda. According to the League, however, its members were targeted for engaging in political mobilization. Their “crime,” the organization said, was “nothing more than standing up, in public, for the dignity of the working people of Uganda.” “For this, they were seized, detained, and held against their will by a state apparatus that fears the organized power of its own people,” the League said. Allegations of mistreatment The League alleges that the arrested members were severely beaten while in detention. Those involved in securing their release said they remained concerned about their physical condition, with the detainees reportedly not feeling well following their treatment in custody. The League said the detained members were eventually released following pressure and mobilization from supporters in Uganda and abroad. “We are relieved to report that, following sustained pressure, mobilization, and the unrelenting demands of comrades both at home and abroad, all those detained have now been released,” the statement said. But the organization insists that it did not regard the release as an end to the matter. “But their freedom was not given, it was extracted, bitterly and only after our collective refusal to remain silent,” the League said. League calls out wider repression The Communist League of Uganda said the arrests should be understood within a wider political context. “This arrest did not occur in a vacuum,” the League said. “It is part of a broader pattern of state repression against organizers, trade unionists, and left political movements across Uganda who dare to challenge entrenched power, corruption, and the economic order that keeps the majority of our people in poverty while a small elite enriches itself.” The organization argued that the criminalization of political mobilization was directly connected to the ability of working people to organize collectively. “Mass mobilization is criminalized precisely because it is effective, because when working people organize and raise their voices together, they threaten the interests that depend on their silence and division,” it said. The League further said that the arrests represented an attempt to discourage political organizing beyond the individuals detained. “The targeting of Comrades Twahala, Odeke, and Namususwa is an attack not just on three individuals, but on the right of all Ugandans to organize, assemble, and demand a better future,” the statement said. “It is an attempt to instill fear in our ranks and to deter others from joining the struggle. We say clearly it will not work.” Calls for political freedoms Following the arrests, the Communist League of Uganda demanded an end to what it described as harassment and surveillance of its members and other activists involved in peaceful political organizing. Read more: Uganda’s largest non-state media group under military siege The League called for guarantees of the constitutional rights to freedom of assembly, expression and political association for all Ugandan citizens. It also demanded that any remaining charges or conditions imposed on the released members be dropped. The organization appealed to communist, socialist and progressive organizations internationally to publicize what it described as an act of repression. “We call upon fraternal communist, socialist, and progressive organizations across the world to publicize this act of repression through your own networks, publications, and platforms,” the statement said. The Communist Party Marxist of Kenya also expressed solidarity with the Communist League of Uganda and called for the release of its members. Arrests follow inaugural congress Notably, the arrests came immediately after the Communist League of Uganda’s inaugural National Congress, at a moment when the organization is attempting to consolidate its structures and expand its political work. The emergence of the League adds another left-wing organization to Uganda’s contested political realities, where opposition politicians, activists, trade unionists and civil society groups have raised concerns over restrictions on political organizing and public assembly. The political environment has also included the continued detention of opposition figure Kizza Besigye, whose case has drawn international attention and renewed scrutiny of political freedoms in Uganda.

articles.title: Operation Southern Spear: uncovering the CIA’s killing spree in Latin America

articles.content: A drone hovering over a burning Ecuadorian fishing boat hours after it was bombed belonged to a San Diego-based defense contractor with an $800 million contract with the US Navy. Investigative journalist Camila Lourdes Galarza tells Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek that boat was one of three unarmed fishing vessels bombed in what the Washington Post later confirmed was part of a covert CIA program to kill “suspected drug traffickers” in the Pacific – without any oversight or public acknowledgment. As Operation Southern Spear marks its first year, Galarza breaks down how Ecuadorian President and Miami-born billionaire Daniel Noboa has turned his country into a testing ground for US military expansion under Trump’s Donroe Doctrine: from former Blackwater mercenaries at polling stations, to martial law decrees shielding US troops from Ecuadorian law, to the SOUTHCOM general she says admitted the real target of all of this is Ecuador’s lithium stores and rare earth minerals. Galarza connects the boat strikes, on which she reported extensively for Drop Site News, to a much larger pattern, linking Fernando Cerimedo’s CIA and Israel ties to a US embassy plot to interfere in Colombia’s elections, to the assassination in June of Ecuadorian prosecutor Alexandra Bravo as US troops patrolled the streets. articles.title: US strikes hit wedding in Iran as death toll from latest strikes crosses 18
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: At least 18 Iranians, including children, were killed and around 80 others were injured in the latest US airstrikes in southern Iran’s Khuzestan, Bushehr, Baluchestan, and Hormozgan provinces late on the night of Tuesday, September 1, IRNA reported. Several Iranian media reports claimed one of the sites attacked on Tuesday night was a wedding celebration in Sirik in the southern Hormozgan province. At least four people, including a four years old child, were killed and around 70 others were wounded in that attack. Meanwhile, Iran rejected the claims made by the US Central Command that the overnight attacks only targeted locations belonging to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in retaliation to attacks on commercial ships and US servicemen in the region. On Wednesday morning, Iran retaliated by striking US military outposts in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, and Iraq with drones and missiles. The IRGC also claimed it downed yet another US MQ-9 drone. The IRGC said its retaliatory attacks on Kuwait have “killed a number of enemy elements.” The latest round of military strikes and counter strikes in the over six-month-long war on Iran began on Sunday when US forces carried out attacks on Iran’s Larak island on Sunday, killing scores of Iranians. The military strikes on Larak Island were carried out after a weeks-long halt in military hostilities. The Trump administration in the US had previously claimed it would prioritize economically isolating Iran instead of carrying out further attacks. After Sunday’s strikes, US CENTCOM said the attacks were part of its efforts to prevent Iran from laying fresh mines in the Strait of Hormuz in the future. Iran ridiculed Washington’s claims, calling them a “fantasy” and retaliated by striking US military bases in Jordan and the UAE. In a statement issued late Tuesday night, the IRGC claimed that the “desperate” attacks carried out by the US would only tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz instead of weakening it in any way. The IRGC also claimed two oil tankers hit a mine and caught fire while trying to use the US-backed route to cross the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. At least two crew members were reported killed in the incident. The cycle of US atrocities Responding to the latest attacks on civilians in Iran, Esmail Baghaei, official spokesperson of its foreign ministry called it a completion of the “catalogue of atrocities” carried out by the US since the attack on school children in Minab on the first day of the war. More than 160 school children were killed in the strike in Minab on February 28. In a similar strike on the same day, 21 civilians were killed in Lamerd sports hall. Following the global outrage, the US initially denied the attacks and later dismissed them as “human errors,” refusing to hold those responsible accountable. The targeting of civilians during war is a war crime. “More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalization of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy,” Baghaei said, vowing a strong response to the attacks. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of the Iranian parliament and head of its delegation negotiating peace terms, condemned the latest attacks on civilians. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan,” Ghalibaf wrote in a post on X , comparing attacks on the wedding celebration with attacks in Minab and Lamerd sports hall. Over 3,500 Iranians, including its former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and several other top military and political leaders, have been killed in the war started by the US and Israel. The war has also heavily impacted the global economy. The Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global trade in energy, has been blocked for months now causing a rise in global energy prices. International efforts to end the war have failed after the US refused to adhere to the norms of the peace agreement, called the Memorandum of Understanding, signed in June. Iran has recently reiterated that if the US agrees to adhere to all the provisions of the MoU the situation in the region would be resolved, which may include the normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
